title: What’s Behind the Heat Wave Scorching Huge Parts of the World
gist: Simultaneous record heat across Western Europe, the western US and East Asia is being driven by a stack of reinforcing mechanisms: a wavy jet stream locking heat domes in place, ocean temperatures that have absorbed ~90 percent of trapped heat, downwind energy from Category 5 Hurricane Genevieve, and an El Niño that formed only in June yet is already pacing ahead of any previously observed strong event — on top of a baseline that has already warmed more than 1.5 degrees Celsius.

insights.claim: Western Europe recorded its hottest June on record and record-breaking wildfires in July, with hundreds of heat records falling from Spain to Germany before a further round of extreme temperatures arrived.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Back-to-back record months rather than isolated events mean European power demand, agricultural output and insured wildfire losses are all being repriced within a single season.
insights.quote: Western Europe endured its hottest June on record and record-breaking wildfires in July.
insights.locator: Western Europe endured its hottest June on record

insights.claim: French president Emmanuel Macron described the combination of extreme heat and intense wildfires as creating the toughest situation France has faced since the Second World War.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A head-of-state framing at that intensity typically precedes emergency fiscal response and accelerated climate-adaptation spending.
insights.quote: the one-two punch of high heat and intense wildfires are creating a dangerous situation, which he called “the toughest since the Second World War.”
insights.locator: On Tuesday, French president Emanuel Macron said

insights.claim: The western US faces heat from the California coast to the Rockies with Phoenix forecast up to 115°F (46°C), Salt Lake City at a potentially record 106°F, and parts of Montana under extreme heat watch at up to 110°F.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Simultaneous extremes across the interior West stress the same grid interconnections at once, removing the regional diversity that normally lets utilities import power.
insights.quote: Temperatures in Phoenix are expected to reach up to 115 degrees Fahrenheit (46 degrees Celsius), while Salt Lake City could see a record-breaking high of 106 Fahrenheit.
insights.locator: The western US is also bracing for high heat

insights.claim: Hot, dry conditions in Montana have the potential to supercharge fires already burning in the state, compounding heat risk with active wildfire risk.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Heat events layered onto active fire complexes are where utility liability and insurer loss tails concentrate.
insights.quote: The hot and dry conditions have the potential to supercharge some of the fires already burning across that state.
insights.locator: Montana is also under an extreme heat watch

insights.claim: Interior Western US cities are running at or near record temperatures for early August, which is notable because that period is already climatologically among the hottest of the year.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
entities: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
insights.so_what: Records set against an already-high seasonal baseline indicate genuine tail-risk conditions rather than a shifted calendar.
insights.quote: All of these interior Western cities will be at our near record temperatures for early August, which is saying something—it's a pretty hot time of the year to begin with, so it's a fairly high bar
insights.locator: says Daniel Swain, a climate scientist

themes.theme: Overnight lows as the hidden risk variable

insights.claim: Phoenix overnight temperatures are forecast not to drop much below 100°F, and the city recently tied its record for highest low temperature at 97°F — removing the nighttime recovery window that limits heat mortality.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Nighttime minimums, not daytime peaks, drive both heat deaths and 24-hour cooling load — the metric to track for utility overnight demand and public-health response.
insights.quote: The city tied the record for its highest low temperature last Thursday, with temperatures bottoming out at 97 degrees Fahrenheit.
insights.locator: Overnight temperatures in some of these places are forecast to be unusually high

themes.theme: Jet stream and heat dome mechanics

insights.claim: The temperature extremes are being produced by heat domes — high-pressure areas that lock in sunny skies and warmth — and the reason so many are stationary at once is the shape of the jet stream that creates and steers most northern hemisphere weather.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Jet stream waviness is the upstream variable to watch: it determines whether extremes are brief and mobile or persistent and stacked across regions.
insights.quote: The band of air that blows from west to east around the northern hemisphere “creates and steers most of the weather we experience,”
insights.locator: The sweltering temperatures are being driven in part by a series of heat domes

insights.claim: When the jet stream becomes wavy, tropical air pushes northward and gets locked over normally temperate regions, which is the mechanism importing heat from abnormally warm seas into Europe.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: This mechanism explains why European heat events are increasingly persistent rather than transient — duration, not peak, is the risk driver for crops and grids.
insights.quote: When the jet stream becomes wavy, that can allow tropical air to push northward and get locked in place over areas that are usually more temperate.
insights.locator: When the jet stream becomes wavy

insights.claim: Sea temperatures around Europe are anomalously high and are directly linked to accumulated heat-trapping carbon pollution, roughly 90 percent of which has gone into the ocean rather than the atmosphere.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: The 90 percent ocean fraction means decades of stored heat will keep feeding marine heatwaves regardless of near-term emissions paths — a structural, not cyclical, input.
insights.quote: The seas all around Europe are running a fever
insights.locator: In Europe’s case, the jet stream is bringing extra heat

insights.claim: Oceans around Japan and China are also unusually warm, supplying the same heat-reservoir mechanism to the East Asian heat waves affecting South Korea and Japan.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Warm seas on both sides of the northern hemisphere means Asian and European heat events are correlated, not independent — a diversification failure for weather-exposed portfolios.
insights.quote: Francis also points out that the oceans around Japan and China are also unusually warm, helping to fuel the heat waves there.
insights.locator: About 90 percent of that trapped heat goes into the ocean

insights.claim: The western US heat wave is partly a downwind effect of Hurricane Genevieve, a Category 5 storm that built over warm ocean waters off Mexico and is injecting a pulse of heat and energy into the atmosphere.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Tropical cyclone activity now propagates into continental heat risk, linking hurricane season forecasts to inland power-demand forecasts.
insights.quote: The western US heat wave is due in part to downwind effects of Hurricane Genevieve, a Category 5 hurricane that built up over warm ocean waters off the coast of Mexico this week.
insights.locator: Regional weather is also playing a role

themes.theme: An unprecedented El Niño on a warmed baseline

insights.claim: This year's El Niño formed in the Pacific only in June yet is already pacing well ahead of how developed previous strong El Niños were at the same point in the year, and is forecast to be exceptionally strong.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: An early, fast-developing El Niño pulls forward its global impacts — relevant for agricultural commodity positioning that normally assumes a multi-month lag.
insights.quote: But this year’s El Niño is forecast to be exceptionally strong, and it’s already pacing well ahead of how developed other strong El Niños were at this time of year.
insights.locator: El Niño affects weather patterns around the world

insights.claim: The combination of a record-pace El Niño with a baseline global temperature already more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels means impacts may be both more intense and earlier than the historical playbook implies.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Historical El Niño analogues understate the coming impact because no prior event started from this baseline — models calibrated on past cycles will be biased low.
insights.quote: Swain says that fact, combined with the fact that the world has already warmed more than 1.5 degrees Celsius, means that we may see more intense El Niño impacts, and they may come on sooner than expected.
insights.locator: But this year’s El Niño is forecast to be exceptionally strong

insights.claim: A leading climate scientist expects this to be the strongest El Niño ever observed by a significant margin and a completely unprecedented event, extreme enough to challenge existing scientific understanding of the phenomenon.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A record El Niño is the single highest-conviction macro weather call in the piece, with direct read-through to grains, cocoa, energy demand and catastrophe reinsurance pricing into 2027.
insights.quote: This really is looking like shaping up to be the strongest El Niño we've ever observed by a significant margin
insights.locator: The forecast is so extreme, it could challenge what scientists know

insights.claim: A recent attribution analysis concluded that June's European heat wave, which killed more than 1,000 people, would not have been possible without the additional atmospheric heat from burning fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Attribution studies that rule out natural-variability explanations are the evidentiary basis for climate litigation and for regulatory exposure at fossil fuel producers.
insights.quote: A recent analysis found that the heat wave that hit Europe in June and left more than 1,000 people dead would not have been possible without the extra heat that burning fossil fuels has added to the atmosphere.
